name: Betteridge's Law of Headlines
statement: Any headline that ends in a question mark can be answered by the word no.
meaning: When a headline asks a yes/no question, the honest answer is almost always no — otherwise it would have been stated as a fact.
mechanism: A publisher confident the answer is yes writes the assertion outright, because a strong claim earns more attention. Phrasing it as a question is a hedge: it lets the piece imply a sensational 'yes' while staying deniable when the evidence does not support it. The question mark is a tell that the evidence fell short.

examples.text: The maxim's namesake case was a TechCrunch headline Betteridge criticised: 'Did Last.fm Just Hand Over User Listening Data To the RIAA?' The answer was no — Last.fm denied it — and the question mark was doing the work a fact could not.
'Is this the phone that finally kills the iPhone?' By Betteridge's Law: no. Had it actually killed the iPhone, the headline would have simply said so, in the declarative, and taken the credit.

variants.name: Marr's formulation (2004)
variants.text: The journalist Andrew Marr stated the idea years earlier in My Trade: 'If the headline asks a question, try answering no.' The principle was 'an old truism among journalists' well before it acquired Betteridge's name.

variants.name: Davis's law
variants.text: A 1991 compilation of Murphy's-law variants recorded the same principle as 'Davis's law' — though who 'Davis' was is genuinely unknown. Evidence the observation was folklore long before it was named.

whyItMatters: It is a fast filter for clickbait and overclaiming: an interrogative headline usually signals a story that could not support the assertion it wants you to infer. It trains a healthy scepticism about how information is packaged.

working.lead: Read the question mark as a hedge
working.text: treat an interrogative headline as an admission that the piece can only imply its claim, not assert it.

working.lead: Ask why they didn't just say it
working.text: if the answer were a confident yes, the outlet would run the stronger declarative headline and take the credit — so the question form is a tell.
look for evidence that would justify the assertion; usually the article never delivers it.
the rule is about interrogatives that smuggle a claim, not genuine open questions ('How does X work?'), where it does not apply.

limits: It is a humorous heuristic, not a law of logic: plenty of question-headlines are honestly answered 'yes', and it only bears on yes/no framings, not genuine open questions. Studies bear out the caveat — an analysis of question-titled scholarly articles found many were answered 'yes', not 'no', because academic questions are real inquiries rather than clickbait hedges. And the rule survives partly on selection bias: the memorable confirming cases (the overclaiming tabloid headline) stick, while the many question-headlines answered 'yes' or 'maybe' are quietly forgotten.
misreadings: It is a rule of thumb about journalistic incentives, not a law of logic — plenty of question-headlines do have the answer 'yes', and honest explainers legitimately pose questions. It describes a tendency in how sensational stories are framed, not a guarantee about any single article.
origin: Named for the British technology journalist Ian Betteridge, who stated it on his own blog, Technovia, in a February 2009 post titled 'TechCrunch: Irresponsible journalism' — criticising a TechCrunch story whose question-mark headline the piece could not substantiate. He called it 'my maxim', presenting it as something he had long said rather than a new coinage; similar observations had circulated earlier, including Andrew Marr's 2004 version and the older 'Davis's law'.

sources.text: Betteridge, I. (23 February 2009). 'TechCrunch: Irresponsible journalism.' Technovia. — the post that named the maxim, on Betteridge's own blog.
Marr, A. (2004). My Trade: A Short History of British Journalism. Macmillan. — the earlier 'answer no' formulation.
